clue.text: Help Conservative to hide billions, moving account

indicators.note: you hide a thing by shutting it away inside something bigger, so the letter named next is written into the middle of the piece before it

parts.note: SOS is the distress call, the signal that means send help
b is the everyday shorthand for a billion, as in a company valued at £5b
a Tory is a member of the Conservative party in Britain

explanation.surface: A Tory politician is helped to stash away billions by shifting them from one account to another.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface has a politician quietly salting money away. 'Moving' is the trap: it looks like a shuffling instruction and belongs to the definition, where it means affecting.
explanation.definitionFit: A sob story is a hard-luck tale told to move whoever hears it, so 'moving account' names what it is and what it is for.

clue.text: Species, cross including head of human and every other bit of lion

definitions.text: Species, cross including head of human and every other bit of lion

indicators.note: the outer letters include, or hold inside them, the rest

parts.note: sp. is the standard abbreviation for species in biology
X is the shape of a cross, as on a ballot paper

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: supplies its first letter

indicators.note: every other letter is taken, skipping alternate ones

parts.note: supplies its second and fourth letters

explanation.surface: A description of a hybrid creature built from a human head and a lion's body.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Every other bit of' lion takes its even letters, not the odd ones. Read whole, the clue also describes the creature itself, so it is an &lit.
explanation.definitionFit: The Egyptian sphinx is a mythical hybrid with a human head on the body of a lion.

clue.text: Local worker saving money

parts.note: saving and barring both mean leaving something out — barring accidents, saving your blushes
legal tender is the money a creditor is obliged to accept

explanation.surface: A worker in the neighbourhood is putting money aside.
explanation.walkthrough: Neither word is doing what the surface suggests: one is an old preposition meaning except, the other the legal term for cash. Nobody in this clue is economising.
explanation.definitionFit: Your local is the pub down the road, and the person serving behind its counter is exactly the worker meant.

clue.text: Stick the rug down in Ilkley?

indicators.note: Ilkley is a Yorkshire town, and Yorkshire speech clips the definite article to a bare t', so the words are to be said in that accent

parts.note: Yorkshire drops everything but the opening letter, writing t' where the rest of the country writes the word out
a rug is slang for a hairpiece

explanation.surface: Someone is told to stick the rug down in a Yorkshire town.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is somebody laying a rug flat on the floor. Ilkley Moor is the Yorkshire landmark of the county's best-known song, which is what makes the accent fair.
explanation.definitionFit: A twig is the thinnest stick on a tree, so the plain noun sense of 'stick' is the one being asked for.

clue.text: Try a lie to distort truth

indicators.note: to distort a thing is to pull it out of the shape it came in, and letters pulled about like that will not stay in their given order

parts.note: these three words hand over their seven letters as raw material

explanation.surface: Someone is tempted to tell a lie and bend the truth.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is advice to a witness in the box. 'Truth' sits at the end where a solver expects more wordplay, and it is the definition instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Reality is what is actually the case rather than what is claimed, which is truth in its everyday sense of the facts.

clue.text: Departure for one on ship

parts.note: e.g. is short for the Latin exempli gratia, which is what 'for one' announces
a memo headed 're pay' is about pay, and a row on pay is the same row
SS is the prefix on a steamship's name

explanation.surface: A lone passenger sets off aboard a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: Someone leaving on a boat is the picture, and there is nothing in it: all three words are abbreviations laid end to end, none of them meaning what the sentence says.
explanation.definitionFit: Egress is the formal word for the way out or the act of going out, the noun a fire officer uses where the rest of us say departure.

clue.text: Complain again, hearing that firing range after August 12th?

parts.note: to grouse is to grumble on and on about something

indicators.note: hearing a word puts it in your ear rather than on the page, so you write down whatever spelling sounds the same

parts.note: as much again is as much more, and that little word said aloud is spelt quite differently on the page

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles once more about a firing range as the shooting season opens on August 12th.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firing range' pulls towards a rifle butt at an army camp. The date is what redirects it to a hillside: shooting, not soldiering.
explanation.definitionFit: Red grouse shooting opens on 12 August, the Glorious Twelfth, and the heather upland the guns walk out onto is a grouse moor.

clue.text: Abandoned lover with skill climbing on top

parts.note: an ex is a former partner, one left behind

indicators.note: in a down entry, climbing means the word is written from the bottom upwards

parts.note: art means skill, as in 'the art of conversation'

explanation.surface: A jilted partner, with some talent for it, is clambering on top of things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on top' looks like part of the climbing picture, but it is the definition, meaning additionally; 'climbing' turns the skill word upside down in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Extra means additional, something given over and above the usual, as in 'paid on top'.

clue.text: Quietly interrupting naval chief, talk

definitions.note: The clue offers the plain verb where the answer is an -ing form; the swap works because 'talk' is also a noun for the activity itself, as in straight talk.

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break into something already under way, so the letter lands inside the piece rather than beside it

parts.note: a sea king was a Norse chief who commanded ships, the raiding captain of the sagas
p is the musician's mark for playing softly, from the Italian piano

explanation.surface: Someone softly cuts in on an admiral to have a word.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Naval chief' looks as though it wants a rank — an admiral, a first sea lord. It wants two ordinary words run together instead, and no navy is involved.
explanation.definitionFit: Speaking and talk name the same activity: ask for plain speaking and you are asking for plain talk.

clue.text: Work over, what remains after term for professor?

indicators.note: a term is a boundary or stopping point — think terminus — so the term of a word is the single letter it ends on
what comes after something is written behind it, which puts the letter just found at the front of the assembly

parts.note: the word stops on this letter, and the clue wants nothing else from it
'eh?' and 'what?' are the same request to have something said again
what a fire leaves behind is ash

explanation.surface: What is left for an academic to do once the university term is over?
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is an academic joke about end-of-term leftovers, and 'term' is not the university's. It is the older sense: the limit, the point at which a thing stops.
explanation.definitionFit: To rehash is to go over old material and serve it up again, which is the phrasal verb 'work over' in its reworking sense.

clue.text: Remote location for one affected their game

indicators.note: to affect a thing is to act on it and change it, and letters changed like that come out in a new arrangement

parts.note: these two words hand over their nine letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A solitary spot has put someone off their game.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like a shooting estate someone's hobby has ruined. 'For one' is not counting anything — it is pointing at the single occupant the answer implies.
explanation.definitionFit: A hermitage is the cell a hermit withdraws to, so the phrase covers both the solitude and the single occupant.

clue.text: Oddball dismissed seconds from predicted retirement

parts.note: a batsman given out has been dismissed, and a sacked employee is out too

indicators.note: the seconds are the letters standing second, one taken from each of the two words that follow

parts.note: the second letter of each word in turn, in the order the clue gives them

explanation.surface: An eccentric player is dismissed just seconds before a retirement everyone had predicted.
explanation.walkthrough: Cricket runs under the whole surface — a player dismissed, a retirement forecast — and neither word survives it. One is a synonym, the other a pair of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Outré is French for beyond the bounds, used in English of anything eccentric enough to raise eyebrows — oddball behaviour.

clue.text: Carol never felt unlimited

parts.note: 'never!' in speech is an emphatic refusal, the same answer said harder

indicators.note: a word's limits are the letters at each end, so removing them leaves only what was in the middle

parts.note: the two letters left standing once the outer pair go

explanation.surface: A woman named Carol has never felt free of limits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carol' looks like a woman's name in a sentence about someone who never felt free. It is the definition, and the answer is the French word every carol sheet shouts.
explanation.definitionFit: Noel is French for Christmas, and English borrowed it as the refrain of Christmas songs and then as a word for such a carol.

clue.text: Trace of life left in Sackville-West's grand garden?

indicators.note: the little word puts the letter just named inside the name that follows it, rather than beside it

parts.note: Vita Sackville-West, the writer who made the garden at Sissinghurst, with the clue's possessive s attached
L is the map and stage-direction abbreviation for left
a park is a garden on the grand scale, laid out around a country house

explanation.surface: Some trace of life lingers in Vita Sackville-West's great garden.
explanation.walkthrough: Sissinghurst, the Kent garden Vita Sackville-West made famous, is the picture the surface paints. The clue wants only her first name — and the possessive s that comes with it.
explanation.definitionFit: The vital spark is the flicker of animation that separates the living from the dead, so a trace of life is precisely what it names.

clue.text: Eurovision winner, upset country's losing lead, wails

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means the singer's name is turned upside down

parts.note: Lulu, the Scottish singer, was a joint winner of the Eurovision Song Contest in 1969

indicators.note: losing lead means the word drops its first letter

parts.note: nations are countries; the 's makes it plural

explanation.surface: A Eurovision champion's country loses its lead in the vote, and fans wail.
explanation.walkthrough: LULU turned up gives ULUL; NATIONS losing its first letter gives ATIONS.
explanation.definitionFit: Ululations are long howling cries of grief or celebration.

clue.text: Running, shot and pole? My hero

indicators.note: paint or dye that is running has left its proper place and spread, which is what the letters are told to do

parts.note: the italicised 'and' is one of the words to be used rather than a joiner, so all four hand over their letters

explanation.surface: An admirer lists decathlon events, running, shot put and pole vault, and names their sporting hero.
explanation.walkthrough: Read straight, running, shot and pole are three decathlon events, which is why the sentence holds together. The first of them is really the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Daley Thompson won Olympic decathlon gold in 1980 and 1984, so 'hero' defines by example: he is one rather than a word for one.

clue.text: Constant force cracks nuts as stated

indicators.note: cracking a nut breaks the shell so the contents fall out loose, and the second word carries the sense of deranged as well

parts.note: F is the physics symbol for force, as in F = ma
these two words give up their eight letters to join the F in the mix

explanation.surface: Someone insists, as already stated, that steady force is what cracks nuts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As stated' reads as an instruction to write down what you hear, and that is the trap: the two words are the raw letters, not a sound to be copied.
explanation.definitionFit: Steadfast means fixed and unwavering in position or loyalty, which is constant in the sense of unchanging rather than continual.

clue.text: Spotty son managed to bag kiss

indicators.note: bagging a thing puts it in the bag, so what follows ends up inside the pieces already found

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for son in family records and genealogies
whoever managed the team led it
a peck is a quick kiss on the cheek

explanation.surface: A pimply boy manages to snatch a kiss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Managed to bag' reads as one phrase meaning succeeded in getting. It is two separate instructions, and pulling them apart is the whole job.
explanation.definitionFit: Speckled means marked all over with small spots, so spotty is the plain adjective for the same patterning.

clue.text: Builder's facing police officer, 100 mph in left lane

parts.note: port is the left-hand side of a ship as you face the bow

indicators.note: everything named before this word goes inside the words that come after it, not alongside them

parts.note: the word is taken whole and then broken open near its end to admit what follows
DS is a detective sergeant in the British police
doing a ton is British slang for a hundred miles an hour

explanation.surface: A builder faces a traffic cop after being caught doing 100 mph in the left lane.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a speeding driver watching a police car in the mirror. 'Facing' is the builders' word for the outer skin of a wall, not the way anyone is pointing.
explanation.definitionFit: Portland stone is the pale limestone quarried on Dorset's Isle of Portland and used to face St Paul's — a builder's facing material.

clue.text: Land with many inlets, as if cut by river

indicators.note: a place cut by water has it running through the middle, so the letter goes inside rather than after

parts.note: 'as if!' is the same sarcastic refusal to believe a thing as the two words it stands in for
R is the map-maker's abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A coastline so full of inlets it looks as if a river carved it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut by river' looks as if it wants a river's name — the Exe and the Po are crossword regulars. It wants the single letter that maps use.
explanation.definitionFit: Norway's western coast is cut into thousands of fjords, so no country better answers to a land of many inlets.

clue.text: Dock's our standard base behind seafront, mostly

indicators.note: behind means the base number comes after the seaside word
mostly means most of the word is used, its last letter dropped

parts.note: the seafront is the shore
we count in base ten

explanation.surface: A harbour boasting that its standard base lies just back from the waterfront.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dock' looks like a harbour noun, but it is the verb: to cut short.
explanation.definitionFit: To dock a tail or wages is to cut it back, which is to make it shorter.

clue.text: Mean person you'd be pleased to see go

parts.words: person you'd be pleased to see
parts.note: a pal is a friend, and a friend is who you are pleased to see
have a go at it and have a try at it are the same invitation

explanation.surface: A stingy person is someone you would be glad to see leave.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one sentence about somebody you would rather see the back of. It splits after 'see', and the last word is a noun, not the verb it looks like.
explanation.definitionFit: Paltry means contemptibly small — mean in the sense of meagre or shabby, as in a paltry sum, not mean as in unkind.

clue.text: Prepare to deep-fry Mars bars for Spooner, whose utterances keep coming

indicators.note: for Spooner says the opening sounds of the two words are swapped, as the Reverend Spooner famously did

parts.note: food is coated in batter before deep-frying
Mars bars are chocolate bars, in British slang chocs, which sounds the same as chox

explanation.surface: A cook readies chocolate bars for the deep-fryer, a famously Scottish treat.
explanation.walkthrough: A deep-fried Mars bar is a Scottish chip-shop snack. BATTER CHOCS with the B and CH sounds swapped by 'for Spooner' gives CHATTER BOCS, said like BOX.
explanation.definitionFit: A chatterbox is a person who talks incessantly, someone whose words never stop.

clue.text: African dictator smuggling diamonds, mundane business

indicators.note: a smuggler carries the goods concealed inside something innocent, so the letter travels within the other piece

parts.note: Idi Amin seized power in Uganda in 1971 and ruled it for eight years
D is the card player's abbreviation for the diamonds suit

explanation.surface: An African dictator smuggles diamonds as part of his everyday business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Business' is not commerce here but the day's chores, and the smuggled gems of the surface leave nothing behind but a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Admin is the paperwork and organising that must be got through before anything interesting happens — dull routine, which is what mundane business means.

clue.text: Bride arranged the setting for fantasy

indicators.note: one thing set inside another has that thing as its setting, so the words before are the frame and the letters sit in them

parts.note: four consecutive letters run across the join between these two words

explanation.surface: A bride plans the venue for a fairytale wedding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arranged' is exactly the word that makes a solver start rearranging, and nothing here is to be rearranged: the letters are wanted just as they already stand.
explanation.definitionFit: An idea can be a mere notion or fancy — something dreamed up rather than established — and that is the sense of fantasy wanted.

clue.text: Large item from IKEA perhaps unfinished until now

indicators.note: an unfinished word stops short, losing its last letter

parts.note: so far means up to this point, until now

explanation.surface: Flat-pack furniture from the Swedish store still isn't assembled.
explanation.walkthrough: IKEA is the Swedish flat-pack furniture chain, and 'unfinished' fits its self-assembly items, but here it drops the R from SO FAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A sofa is a big upholstered seat, the kind of bulky furniture a store like IKEA sells.

clue.text: Book to be collected by car, where you're put on hold?

indicators.note: if the car collects you then you travel inside it, so the letter goes within the other piece

parts.note: a limo is the long hired car of airport pickups and weddings

explanation.surface: Someone books a car to collect them and is then left waiting on hold.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the definition is a picture rather than a dictionary entry: suspended, waiting, neither one thing nor the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Limbo in Catholic theology is the waiting place on the edge of hell, so anything stalled and going nowhere is said to be in limbo.

clue.text: Since fish nets unavailable, one loses weight on ship

parts.note: since and as both mean because

indicators.note: a net closes round whatever it catches, so the letters that follow are trapped inside the piece before them

parts.note: the trout is the freshwater fish of every angling picture
n/a is what a form prints where something is not available

explanation.surface: With no fishing nets available, a sailor on board ship loses weight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ship' is a spacecraft and 'loses weight' is free fall rather than dieting, so the definition is a small joke that only lands once the answer is in.
explanation.definitionFit: In orbit there is nothing for a set of scales to push against, so a ship is the one place a person genuinely loses weight.

clue.text: Return wrong filling delivered for pastry

indicators.note: this is an across entry, so a piece that returns is read from its far end back towards the start
whatever fills a thing sits inside it, so those letters go into the middle of the other word

parts.note: a woman who had a baby delivered it, and the two verbs are interchangeable there
a sin is a wrong, the moral sort

explanation.surface: Someone sends back a pastry delivered with the wrong filling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Filling' looks like part of the pastry and is really an instruction, and once the letters are assembled the whole lot has to be read the other way round.
explanation.definitionFit: A Danish is the pastry itself, the iced and fruited kind, named for the country its recipe was borrowed from.

clue.text: Foot part of insect eaten by cook

parts.note: to be part of something is to be in it, and the little word is taken at face value

indicators.note: whatever is eaten ends up inside the eater, so those letters are enclosed by the ones that follow

parts.note: to fry is to cook in hot fat
the ant is the crossword's insect of choice, and a hard-working one

explanation.surface: A bit of an insect gets eaten by a cook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part of' is doing letter work rather than joining the words either side of it, which is easy to read straight past on the way to the insect.
explanation.definitionFit: In military usage the foot is the infantry — the soldiers who march rather than ride — as in an army of horse and foot.
